def: bad-tempered, argumentative, and hard to deal with, often as a lasting habit
ex: The cantankerous old landlord complained about every repair request Priya submitted.
After a sleepless night, Diego was cantankerous with everyone at the morning meeting.

cloze.s: The ___ neighbor yelled at kids for stepping on his lawn and argued with the mail carrier daily.

note: Often used humorously, especially about older people.

def: irritable and hard to control; likely to quarrel, cause trouble, or split into disagreement
ex: The fractious toddler refused his nap and threw his cup across the kitchen.
Negotiations stalled because the coalition was fractious, with each group distrusting the others.

cloze.s: The committee meetings grew so ___ that members shouted over one another and two of them resigned.

def: deeply embarrassing and shameful, especially in a public way that damages someone's dignity
ex: The champion suffered an ignominious defeat, losing in the first round to an unranked player.
After the scandal, the executive made an ignominious exit, escorted out of the building by security.

cloze.s: The team's ___ season ended with zero wins and a last-place finish that fans still joke about.

def: having a long-established habit or trait that is very unlikely to change
ex: Malik is an inveterate gambler who visits the casino every weekend despite his losses.
My aunt, an inveterate optimist, insisted the rain would clear before the picnic started.

cloze.s: After forty years of smoking two packs a day, Olga was a truly ___ smoker who doubted she could ever quit.

note: Usually describes a person by a habit (inveterate liar, inveterate traveler); often, but not always, negative.

def: used as an artificial and usually inferior substitute for the real thing; imitation
ex: During the wartime shortage, people brewed ersatz coffee from roasted chicory and acorns.
The theme park's ersatz Venice had canals and gondolas but none of the real city's charm.

cloze.s: The restaurant served ___ crab made from processed white fish, though the menu implied it was the real thing.

note: From the German word for 'substitute'; usually implies lower quality.

def: willing to act dishonestly in exchange for money or bribes; open to corruption
ex: The venal inspector approved unsafe buildings for anyone who slipped him cash.
Reporters exposed a venal system in which some judges sold favorable rulings to wealthy clients.

cloze.s: The ___ official was arrested for accepting bribes to award city contracts to his friends.

note: Not the same as *venial* (minor and forgivable), as in 'a venial sin.'

def: happening by lucky chance in a way that turns out to be good or useful
ex: Their serendipitous meeting on a delayed train led to a successful business partnership.
Aisha made a serendipitous discovery: a rare first edition sitting in a thrift-store bin.

cloze.s: Finding my lost wedding ring while planting tomatoes was a ___ surprise I never expected.

def: extremely idealistic and romantic in a way that is impractical or unrealistic
ex: His quixotic campaign to abolish all homework in the district never gained any support.
Sofia launched a quixotic plan to restore the old sailboat by herself in a single summer.

cloze.s: Trying to read every book in the city library before retiring was a noble but ___ goal.

note: From Don Quixote, Cervantes's idealistic hero who attacks windmills he believes are giants.

def: relevant and appropriate to the subject being discussed
ex: The judge ruled that the witness's comments were not germane to the case.
Please keep your questions germane to the budget; we'll discuss hiring next week.

cloze.s: Her personal travel stories, though entertaining, weren't ___ to the workplace safety training.

def: confident, stylish, and charming, usually describing a well-dressed man
ex: In a tailored navy suit, the debonair host greeted every guest by name.
Kwame looked debonair at the wedding, cracking jokes and dancing with easy grace.

cloze.s: With his slicked-back hair and smooth charm, the ___ actor seemed born to play a gentleman spy.

def: living a careless, immoral life devoted to heavy drinking, gambling, or other excess
ex: The novel follows a dissolute heir who wastes his fortune on parties and card games.
After years of dissolute living, he quit drinking and began rebuilding his health.

cloze.s: The biography describes the poet's ___ youth of nightly drinking binges and mounting gambling debts.

def: showing no emotion or reaction on the face; calm and expressionless
ex: The defendant remained impassive as the jury foreperson read the verdict aloud.
Yuki kept an impassive face throughout the poker game, giving nothing away.

cloze.s: The palace guard stood ___ while tourists made silly faces and tried to make him laugh.

note: Not the same as *impassioned*, which means full of passion, nearly the opposite.

def: sharp, biting, and harsh in speech or humor; sarcastically critical
ex: The critic's acerbic review called the film 'two hours I will never get back.'
Tomás is known for his acerbic wit, which delights some coworkers and stings others.

cloze.s: Her ___ comments about his cooking left him embarrassed in front of all the dinner guests.

def: clever and skillful, especially in handling difficult situations or using the hands
ex: The adroit negotiator found a deal that both companies could accept.
Fatima was adroit at calming angry customers before small problems escalated.

cloze.s: The surgeon's ___ hands tied the tiny stitches faster than the students could follow.

def: traveling from place to place, especially for work, rather than staying in one location
ex: As a peripatetic music teacher, Liam visits five different schools each week.
Her peripatetic childhood as the daughter of a soldier meant changing schools almost every year.

cloze.s: The ___ journalist filed stories from a dozen countries in a single year, living out of one suitcase.

def: unpleasantly too sweet or too sentimental, to the point of becoming sickening
ex: The frosting was so cloying that Hannah scraped most of it off her slice of cake.
The movie's cloying ending, with everyone hugging in the rain, made the critics groan.

cloze.s: The perfume in the crowded elevator was so heavy and ___ that Wei felt slightly sick.

def: too ready to believe what people say, which makes one easy to trick
ex: Scammers target credulous investors with promises of guaranteed huge returns.
Only the most credulous viewer would believe the late-night commercial for a miracle diet pill.

cloze.s: The ___ tourists paid fifty dollars for a 'genuine' gold watch from a street vendor.

note: Not the same as *credible* (believable): a credulous person believes too easily; a credible story deserves belief.

def: overly dramatic and theatrical in behavior, especially in order to get attention
ex: His histrionic sighs every time he was asked to help annoyed his roommates.
The coach dismissed the player's histrionic fall as an attempt to draw a penalty.

cloze.s: She burst into loud sobs over a tiny scratch on her phone, a ___ display that embarrassed her friends.

def: refusing to change one's views or to compromise, even when others want agreement
ex: Talks collapsed because both sides remained intransigent about the overtime rules.
The intransigent landlord refused every request to delay the rent increase.

cloze.s: Despite hours of debate, Jamal stayed ___, insisting on his plan with no changes at all.

def: easily made angry; having a quick, hot temper
ex: The irascible chef shouted at anyone who touched his knives.
Lack of sleep made Malik irascible, and he snapped at his kids over small things.

cloze.s: The ___ coach threw his clipboard after the very first missed free throw of the game.

def: strongly bringing something to mind, or smelling strongly of something
ex: The old farmhouse was redolent of woodsmoke and freshly baked bread.
Her speech was redolent of an earlier era, full of hope and old-fashioned moral urgency.

cloze.s: The kitchen was ___ of garlic and basil after Sofia spent the afternoon making sauce.

def: eager to fight or start a war; aggressive and hostile
ex: The general's bellicose speeches alarmed the neighboring countries.
After losing the game, a few bellicose fans started shoving people outside the stadium.

cloze.s: The ruler's ___ threats of invasion sent diplomats rushing to calm the crisis.

note: Close to *belligerent*; bellicose stresses an eagerness for war or fighting.

def: done secretly and quietly so that others will not notice
ex: Kwame cast a surreptitious glance at his phone during the wedding toast.
The company made surreptitious changes to its privacy policy without notifying users.

cloze.s: During the exam, she made a ___ attempt to read her neighbor's answers without the teacher noticing.

def: describing conflict within a group or organization that harms its own members
ex: Internecine feuds within the club distracted it from its real goals.
The band split up after years of internecine squabbling over songwriting credits and royalties.

cloze.s: The family business collapsed amid ___ battles among the founder's three children.

note: Originally meant 'deadly to both sides'; today it usually describes infighting within a group.

def: making false, insulting claims meant to damage someone's reputation
ex: The tabloid printed scurrilous rumors about the actor's private life.
Priya sued the blogger for spreading scurrilous accusations about her bakery.

cloze.s: The anonymous flyer made ___ claims that the school principal had stolen money from a charity.

def: lazy and unwilling to work or make an effort
ex: The indolent cat spent the whole afternoon sprawled in a patch of sunlight.
Critics called the new manager indolent because he rarely answered emails or attended meetings.

cloze.s: After an ___ summer of sleeping late and watching TV, Diego struggled to get back to studying.

also: In medicine, describes a condition that progresses slowly or causes little pain.

def: favorable; showing a good chance of success
ex: With interest rates low, it seemed a propitious time to buy a house.
The clear skies and calm winds were a propitious sign for the rocket launch.

cloze.s: Investors waited for a more ___ moment, when markets had calmed, to announce the merger.

def: silly and pointless in a smug or thoughtless way; foolish
ex: The interviewer asked fatuous questions about the scientist's favorite color.
He wore a fatuous grin while ignoring every warning his friends gave him.

cloze.s: The host's ___ remarks, smugly stating the obvious, made the panel of experts roll their eyes.

def: ordinary and everyday; happening daily and often dull
ex: The novel finds beauty in quotidian details like washing dishes and catching the bus.
After the vacation, the quotidian routine of commuting to work felt especially gray.

cloze.s: Her paintings turn ___ objects, such as coffee cups and house keys, into striking works of art.

def: lacking enthusiasm and effort; careless in a relaxed, unconcerned way
ex: The team's lackadaisical defense allowed three easy goals in the first half.
Kwame's lackadaisical approach to filing his taxes earned him a late fee.

cloze.s: Her ___ attitude toward homework, finishing it only whenever she felt like it, worried her parents.

def: extremely unwilling to spend money or use resources; stingy
ex: The parsimonious owner refused to replace the office's broken chairs.
Our parsimonious grandmother saved every rubber band, twist tie, and paper bag.

cloze.s: Liam was so ___ that he reused tea bags three times and never turned on the heat.

also: In science, a parsimonious explanation is the simplest one that fits the facts.

def: cheerful and overflowing with energy and enthusiasm
ex: The ebullient host greeted everyone at the door with hugs and laughter.
Fatima was ebullient after hearing she had passed her nursing exams.

cloze.s: The ___ crowd cheered and danced in the streets after the team won the championship.

def: too eager to please or obey people with power; excessively flattering
ex: The obsequious waiter kept bowing and praising the wealthy diners.
Jamal disliked the obsequious way his coworker agreed with every word the boss said.

cloze.s: The ___ assistant laughed loudly at all of the director's jokes, even the ones that weren't funny.

def: eager to argue or fight; combative
ex: The pugnacious little terrier barked at dogs three times its size.
Her pugnacious interviewing style made guests nervous on the talk show.

cloze.s: Known for his ___ temperament, the boxer picked arguments even at polite press conferences.

def: talking a great deal, especially about unimportant things
ex: The garrulous taxi driver told us his whole life story on the way to the airport.
Normally garrulous, Hannah fell silent when the exam results were announced.

cloze.s: Our ___ seatmate chatted nonstop for the entire six-hour flight.

def: lacking a plan, purpose, or enthusiasm; moving aimlessly from one thing to another
ex: They made desultory conversation while waiting for the delayed train.
After a desultory search of the parking lot, the guard gave up looking for the lost keys.

cloze.s: Bored and tired, Wei flipped through the magazine in a ___ way, barely reading a single page.

def: shy and lacking self-confidence; hesitant to speak up or assert oneself
ex: The diffident student rarely raised her hand, though she usually knew the answers.
Malik gave a diffident smile when his colleagues praised his presentation.

cloze.s: Too ___ to ask for a raise, Olga waited years for her manager to offer one.

def: difficult to understand because it is complex, specialized, or obscure
ex: The professor's abstruse lecture on quantum theory left most students lost.
Tax law is so abstruse that many people hire an accountant just to file.

cloze.s: The philosopher's ___ arguments required several careful readings before Diego could follow them.

def: to put someone or something in danger
ex: Cutting the safety budget could imperil workers at the chemical plant.
The long drought has imperiled crops across the entire region.

cloze.s: Ignoring the doctor's advice could ___ your recovery after surgery.

def: to go beyond a limit, or to break a moral rule or law
ex: Players who transgress the league's code of conduct will be suspended.
The comedian's jokes transgressed the boundaries of good taste, and the audience fell silent.

cloze.s: The monks believe that anyone who ___ the vow of silence must perform extra chores.

def: to reject an offer, request, or friendly approach bluntly or unkindly
ex: The company rebuffed a takeover bid from its larger rival.
Aisha tried to make peace, but her brother rebuffed every attempt she made.

cloze.s: When Tomás offered to help carry the boxes, his neighbor ___ him with a curt 'I've got it.'

also: Also a noun: 'Her proposal met with a sharp rebuff.'

def: to publicly mock someone or something through satire or ridicule
ex: The comedy show lampoons celebrities and their bizarre habits every week.
Cartoonists have lampooned the city's painfully slow subway construction for years.

cloze.s: The student newspaper ___ the cafeteria's mystery meat in a hilarious fake restaurant review.

also: Also a noun: a piece of writing or art that mocks someone.

def: to treat someone too gently and protectively; to overindulge
ex: Some parents coddle their teenagers by doing all their laundry and homework.
The manager was accused of coddling weak performers instead of setting clear goals.

cloze.s: If you ___ the puppy every time it whines, it will never learn to sleep alone.

also: In cooking, to cook an egg gently in water just below boiling.

def: to interpret or understand words or actions in a particular way
ex: Her silence was construed as agreement by the rest of the team.
Please don't construe my questions as criticism; I'm just curious about the plan.

cloze.s: The judge ___ the contract narrowly, ruling that it did not cover weekend work.

note: Its relative *misconstrue* means to interpret wrongly.

def: to ask someone earnestly or anxiously to do something; to beg
ex: Maria entreated her son to call home more often while he was overseas.
The villagers entreated the government to repair the collapsed bridge before winter.

cloze.s: With tears in her eyes, she ___ the judge to show mercy to her younger brother.

def: to shock or excite people into taking action
ex: The flood galvanized neighbors to build a new levee together.
Her halftime speech galvanized the team after a terrible first half.

cloze.s: News of the factory closing ___ residents to organize a job fair within a week.

also: Technically, to coat iron or steel with zinc to protect it from rust.

def: to have an effect on something, often by limiting or intruding on it
ex: New rules could impinge on employees' freedom to work from home.
Noise from the construction site impinged on our sleep for months.

cloze.s: Yuki worried that the long commute would ___ on the time she spent with her children.

def: to exceed someone or something in amount or ability, or to move faster; surpass
ex: Demand for the new vaccine quickly outstripped the available supply.
Sofia's skills soon outstripped those of her first piano teacher.

cloze.s: On the last lap, the young runner ___ the defending champion and crossed the line first.

def: to break or violate a law, rule, or agreement
ex: Selling alcohol to anyone under twenty-one contravenes state law and can cost a store its license.
The new building contravenes the neighborhood's height restrictions by two full stories.

cloze.s: Sharing customer data without consent would ___ the company's privacy agreement.

def: to praise someone or something with great enthusiasm
ex: Doctors often extol the health benefits of a brisk daily walk.
The review extolled the restaurant's handmade pasta and friendly staff.

cloze.s: In every interview, the coach ___ the hard work of her assistants rather than taking credit herself.

def: to offer or hold out something to someone, such as a hand, gift, or explanation
ex: He proffered his hand in greeting, but she ignored it.
The witness proffered a new explanation for the missing documents.

cloze.s: When the waiter ___ the wine list, Kwame politely waved it away and ordered water.

def: to warn or scold someone firmly, though usually not harshly
ex: The teacher admonished the boys for talking during the fire drill.
Priya's doctor admonished her to take her blood pressure medication every day.

cloze.s: The referee ___ both players for shoving but decided not to send either of them off.

def: to complain about or express sadness over something
ex: Longtime fans bemoan the rising cost of tickets at the ballpark.
Diego bemoaned the loss of his favorite coffee shop when it closed.

cloze.s: Instead of ___ the rainy weather, the campers played board games in the tent.

def: to fix an idea, value, or habit firmly in someone's mind through repeated teaching
ex: The coach inculcated discipline in her players through daily drills.
Parents try to inculcate good manners in their children from an early age.

cloze.s: The program aims to ___ a love of reading in children by sending books home every week.

def: to officially announce a law or rule, or to spread an idea widely
ex: The agency promulgated new safety standards for children's car seats.
Online forums helped promulgate the false rumor across the country within days.

cloze.s: The school board ___ the new dress code by mailing a copy to every family.

def: to make something deliberately unclear or confusing, often to hide the truth
ex: The annual report used jargon to obfuscate the company's mounting losses.
Stop obfuscating with technical terms and answer the question directly, please.

cloze.s: The lawyer tried to ___ the facts with long, confusing explanations that went nowhere.

def: to regard with deep respect and reverence, often because of age or holiness
ex: Many cultures venerate their ancestors with special ceremonies and offerings.
Young jazz musicians still venerate the classic recordings of the 1950s.

cloze.s: The villagers ___ the ancient oak tree, believing it protected the whole community.

def: to erase or completely remove something, such as a record, name, or memory
ex: After five years, the court agreed to expunge his juvenile record.
She tried to expunge the embarrassing photo from every website where it appeared.

cloze.s: The editor ___ every reference to the scandal from the second edition of the book.

def: to entertain or amuse someone with stories, jokes, or lively talk
ex: Grandpa regaled us with tales of his years working on fishing boats.
Hannah regaled her coworkers with stories from her hiking trip to Peru.

cloze.s: At dinner, Jamal ___ his friends with funny stories about his first week as a teacher.

def: to do something one considers beneath one's dignity, often reluctantly or grudgingly
ex: The star barely deigned to sign autographs for the fans waiting in the rain.
She didn't even deign to reply to my polite email.

cloze.s: The celebrity chef finally ___ to visit the dining room after the customers had waited an hour.

note: Often used sarcastically or in the negative: 'He didn't deign to answer.'
